<p class="dq-context">A deal is only the start. Will you work with one investor who gives you full attention, or share your company with several? Before you plan, you want two numbers: what to expect, and how much reality can differ from it. In other words: what is the expected outcome, and what is the variance of the outcome, the measure of risk that this lecture introduces?</p>

If your pitch ends in a deal, how many sharks will you work with, and how
much does that number differ from deal to deal?

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} **Warm up.** Lecture 2 ended with random variables for the
experiment that selects one record uniformly at random. Define $X=1$ if the
selected pitch reached an on-air deal and $X=0$ otherwise. Now select one of
the 882 deals at random instead. Define $K$ as the number of sharks in the
selected deal (`number_sharks_in_deal`).

1. What are the possible values of $X$ and of $K$?
2. Do these possible values tell us how likely each value is?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your preparation

1. $X$ can take the values 0 and 1. $K$ can take the values 1, 2, 3, 4,
   and 5: every deal has at least one shark, and the panel has five.
2. No. The support lists the possible values. A probability distribution
   must also give a probability to each value. This lecture adds that
   step.
:::

If functions, support, or summation notation are unfamiliar, review

Which option has the higher expected payoff, and which one is riskier?
Choose one answer for each part: A, B, or equal. You find the answer in the

## Lecture material

### Start with a founder's question

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Lecture 2 gave a probability to a single event, such as deal or no deal.
Many business questions are about a number with several possible values
instead. Suppose your pitch ends in a deal. Will you work with one investor
who gives you full attention, or with a group of sharks who share the deal?
The Shark Tank file records the number of sharks in each deal in the
variable `number_sharks_in_deal`. The code below keeps the 882 records with
an on-air deal, counts the deals by the number of sharks, and then turns
the counts into shares of all deals:

```{r}
#| label: b03-sharks-table
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
deals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1)
shark_counts <- table(deals$number_sharks_in_deal)
shark_counts
round(prop.table(shark_counts), 3)
```

The first output gives the counts. Of the 882 deals, 648 have one shark,
203 have two, 22 have three, 3 have four, and 6 have five. The second
output divides each count by 882. As shares: 0.735, 0.230, 0.025, 0.003,
and 0.007. So almost three in four deals are made with a single shark, and
deals with three or more sharks are rare.

#### Four questions, answered from the shares

1. **How likely is a deal with exactly one shark?** Read it from the shares: 73.5%.
2. **How likely is a deal with at most two sharks?** Add the first two
   shares: 73.5% + 23.0% = 96.5%.
3. **How many sharks should you expect?** Multiply each number by its share
   and add the results:
   $$1\times0.735+2\times0.230+3\times0.025+4\times0.003+5\times0.007\approx1.32.$$
   No deal has 1.32 sharks. The section on expectation
   explains how to read such a number.
4. **How much do deals differ from that number?** Not much: most deals have
   one shark and nearly all others have two. The section on variance
   teaches how to summarise this spread in one number.

Question 4 is about risk. The money choice in the Lecture 1 survey had the
same average payoff for all three options, and the options differed only
in how far a single result could lie from that average. The variance turns
this idea into a number.

Each of the four answers uses a tool that has a name. The list of shares is a probability mass
function. The running total in question 2 is a cumulative distribution
function. The weighted average in question 3 is an expected value. The spread
in question 4 is measured by the variance and the standard deviation. These
four tools are introduced below, one section each, starting with the list
of shares.

### A PMF assigns probability to each possible value

<p class="concept-video"><strong>MIT explanation (review):</strong>
<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zW1_iugJvF0">05.3 Probability Mass Functions</a>.</p>

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} A random variable tells us which numerical values we may observe. Its
distribution adds the missing information: how the probability is divided
between those values.

For a discrete random variable $X$, the **probability mass function (PMF)**
is

$$p_X(x)=P(X=x).$$

Read this notation in parts:

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $X$ | the random variable |
| $x$ | one possible numerical value |
| $p_X$ | the PMF belonging to $X$ |
| $p_X(x)$ | the probability that $X$ equals exactly $x$ |

The probability of one value is also called its probability mass, or mass
for short. A valid PMF must meet two rules:

$$
p_X(x)\ge 0\quad\text{for every }x,
\qquad
\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_X(x)=1,
$$

where $\mathcal X$ is the support of $X$. The first rule prevents negative
probability. The second says that one of the possible values must occur.

::: {#exm-b03-deal-pmf}
## Worked example: the deal-indicator PMF, checked

In the uniform selection experiment from Lecture 2, the deal indicator
$X$ has support $\{0,1\}$. The Shark Tank file has 882 deals among 1,441
records, so 559 records have no deal. The PMF is

$$
p_X(0)=\frac{559}{1441}\approx 0.388,
\qquad
p_X(1)=\frac{882}{1441}\approx 0.612.
$$

Check both rules: each mass is non-negative, and

$$
\frac{559}{1441}+\frac{882}{1441}=\frac{1441}{1441}=1.
$$

This is a valid PMF.
:::

R can do the same calculation in three steps. First, `mean()` of the 0/1
column `deal_on_show` gives the share of records with a deal, which we
store as `p_hat` for later use. Second, `table()` counts the records with
the values 0 and 1, and `prop.table()` divides each count by the 1,441
records. Third, `sum()` adds the two masses to check the second rule.

```{r}
#| label: b03-deal-pmf
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
p_hat <- mean(sharks$deal_on_show)   # 882/1441

deal_pmf <- prop.table(
  table(factor(sharks$deal_on_show, levels = c(0, 1)))
)
names(deal_pmf) <- c("0: no on-air deal", "1: on-air deal")
deal_pmf
sum(deal_pmf)
```

The first output is the PMF: 0.388 for no deal and 0.612 for a deal, the
same two fractions as in the worked example. The second output, 1, confirms
that the masses add up to 1. In words: a pitch drawn at random from the file
reached a deal with probability 0.612, so about three in five recorded
pitches ended in a deal. @fig-b03-deal-pmf draws this PMF.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b03-deal-pmf
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "See the R code for this figure"
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-cap: "The PMF of the deal indicator X: two probability masses, at 0 (no on-air deal) and at 1 (on-air deal). The labels show how each height is calculated."
#| fig-alt: "Two vertical bars. At 0 the bar has height 559/1441, about 0.388. At 1 the bar has height 882/1441, about 0.612."
library(ggplot2)
deal_df <- data.frame(
  x = c(0, 1),
  probability = c(559, 882) / 1441,
  label = c("559/1441\n= 0.388", "882/1441\n= 0.612")
)

ggplot(deal_df, aes(x = x, y = probability)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = x, yend = 0),
               linewidth = 1.3, colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.6,
            colour = "#17324D", lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1), limits = c(-0.5, 1.5),
                     labels = c("0: no deal", "1: deal")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.85),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  labs(x = "Value x of the deal indicator", y = expression(p[X](x))) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )
```

The deal indicator has only two possible values, so its PMF has only two
masses. Most business quantities have more possible values. For the number
of sharks $K$ in a randomly selected deal, the PMF gives each number its
share of the 882 deals. The code below takes the counts of the opening
section, divides them by 882 with `prop.table()`, rounds them to three
decimals, and checks that they add up to 1:

```{r}
#| label: b03-sharks-pmf
sharks_pmf <- prop.table(table(deals$number_sharks_in_deal))
round(sharks_pmf, 3)
sum(sharks_pmf)
```

These are the shares from the opening section, now read as probabilities.
If you draw one deal at random, the probability that it has exactly one
shark is 0.735, and the probability that it has five sharks is 0.007, less
than one in a hundred. Both rules hold: every mass is non-negative and the
sum is 1. @fig-b03-sharks-pmf draws this PMF.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b03-sharks-pmf
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "See the R code for this figure"
#| fig-cap: "The PMF of the number of sharks in a randomly selected deal: five separated probability masses, one per possible value. The label above each mass shows its calculation: the number of deals with k sharks divided by all 882 deals."
#| fig-alt: "Five vertical bars at 1 to 5 sharks with heights 648/882 = 0.735, 203/882 = 0.230, 22/882 = 0.025, 3/882 = 0.003 and 6/882 = 0.007."
library(ggplot2)
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
deals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1)
shark_counts <- table(deals$number_sharks_in_deal)
sharks_pmf <- prop.table(shark_counts)
pmf_df <- data.frame(
  k = as.numeric(names(sharks_pmf)),
  probability = as.numeric(sharks_pmf),
  label = sprintf("%d/%d\n= %.3f", as.numeric(shark_counts),
                  sum(shark_counts), as.numeric(sharks_pmf))
)

ggplot(pmf_df, aes(x = k, y = probability)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = k, yend = 0),
               linewidth = 1.3, colour = "#009E73") +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#009E73") +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), vjust = -0.4, lineheight = 0.9,
            size = 3.4, colour = "#17324D") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:5) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.92),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  labs(x = "Number of sharks k", y = expression(p[K](k))) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )
```

The probability mass above 1 in @fig-b03-sharks-pmf has height
$$p_K(1)=P(K=1)=\frac{648}{882}\approx0.735.$$
Almost three quarters of the probability sits on one value. The masses for
three, four, and five sharks are so small that their bars are hard to see.
The label above each bar shows how its height is calculated: the number of
deals with that many sharks, divided by all 882 deals. The
graph shows the PMF as separate probability masses, because $K$ can take
only the listed discrete values. The term probability density function
(PDF) is used only for continuous random variables. Lecture 6 introduces it.

The PMF shows the whole shape of a distribution at a glance: which values
are possible and which of them are likely. Many practical questions,
however, ask about a range of values, such as "at most two sharks". The
next tool answers such questions directly.

### A CDF accumulates probability up to a threshold

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} The PMF asks about one exact value. The **cumulative distribution function
(CDF)** asks how much probability lies at or below a chosen threshold (a
cut-off value). Why do we need a second tool? Many decisions depend on a
threshold. A founder who can handle at most two investors asks for
$P(K\le 2)$. A bank asks how likely sales stay below the level needed to
repay a loan. With the PMF alone, you must add up several masses for every
such question. The CDF stores these sums once, so one reading answers the
question. The two tools carry the same information and are used together.
The PMF shows which single values are likely. The CDF answers questions about
"at most", "at least", and "between". From Lecture 6 on, for continuous
variables, almost every probability is read from a CDF.

Imagine moving from left to right across the PMF and keeping a
running total.

For any random variable $X$,

$$F_X(a)=P(X\le a).$$

Here $a$ is a threshold, not necessarily a value in the support. For a
discrete random variable,

$$F_X(a)=\sum_{x\le a}p_X(x).$$

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="label">Definition</span>

**Probability mass function (PMF)** and **cumulative distribution function
(CDF).** The PMF, $p_X(x)=P(X=x)$, gives the probability that $X$ equals
exactly the value $x$. The CDF, $F_X(a)=P(X\le a)$, gives the probability
that $X$ is at or below the threshold $a$.
:::

#### Try it yourself: build the running total

The lab below shows the PMF of the number of sharks on top and the CDF
below it. Move the slider to change the threshold $a$. Every probability
mass at or below $a$ turns green and is added to the running total. The
lower panel draws the CDF up to the current threshold, and the text below
the panels shows the sum.

<script>
(function () {
  const root = document.getElementById("cdf-lab");
  if (!root || root.dataset.ready) return;
  root.dataset.ready = "true";
  const svg = root.querySelector("#cdf-svg");
  const slider = root.querySelector("#cdf-a");
  const aText = root.querySelector("#cdf-a-text");
  const valueText = root.querySelector("#cdf-value");
  const sumText = root.querySelector("#cdf-sum");
  const counts = [648, 203, 22, 3, 6];
  const total = 882;
  const ks = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
  const ns = "http://www.w3.org/2000/svg";
  const left = 52, right = 440;
  const top1 = 30, bottom1 = 170, top2 = 240, bottom2 = 370;
  const sx = x => left + x / 6 * (right - left);
  const sy1 = p => bottom1 - p / 0.8 * (bottom1 - top1);
  const sy2 = F => bottom2 - F * (bottom2 - top2);
  const add = (name, attrs, parent = svg) => {
    const el = document.createElementNS(ns, name);
    Object.entries(attrs).forEach(([k, v]) => el.setAttribute(k, v));
    parent.appendChild(el); return el;
  };
  const text = (x, y, s, cls, anchor) => {
    const t = add("text", {x: x, y: y, class: cls, "text-anchor": anchor || "middle"});
    t.textContent = s; return t;
  };
  [[top1, bottom1], [top2, bottom2]].forEach(([t, b]) => {
    add("line", {x1: left, y1: b, x2: right, y2: b, class: "b03-axis"});
    add("line", {x1: left, y1: t, x2: left, y2: b, class: "b03-axis"});
    for (let v = 0; v <= 6; v++) {
      add("line", {x1: sx(v), y1: b, x2: sx(v), y2: b + 5, class: "b03-axis"});
      text(sx(v), b + 20, String(v), "b03-tick");
    }
  });
  [0, 0.4, 0.8].forEach(p => text(left - 8, sy1(p) + 4, p.toFixed(1), "b03-tick", "end"));
  [0, 0.5, 1].forEach(F => text(left - 8, sy2(F) + 4, F.toFixed(1), "b03-tick", "end"));
  text(left + 4, top1 - 12, "PMF: P(K = k)", "b03-label", "start");
  text(left + 4, top2 - 12, "CDF: F(a) = P(K ≤ a)", "b03-label", "start");
  text((left + right) / 2, 410, "Number of sharks", "b03-label");
  const bars = ks.map((k, i) => {
    const p = counts[i] / total;
    const h = Math.max(bottom1 - sy1(p), 1.5);
    const r = add("rect", {x: sx(k) - 13, y: bottom1 - h, width: 26, height: h, class: "b03-mass-out"});
    text(sx(k), bottom1 - h - 6, p.toFixed(3), "b03-tick");
    return r;
  });
  const step = add("path", {class: "b03-step"});
  const line = add("line", {y1: top1 - 4, y2: bottom2, class: "b03-threshold"});
  const dot = add("circle", {r: 5, class: "b03-dot"});
  function draw() {
    const a = Number(slider.value);
    let cum = 0, cumCount = 0;
    const parts = [];
    let d = "M " + sx(0) + " " + sy2(0);
    ks.forEach((k, i) => {
      const inside = k <= a + 1e-9;
      bars[i].setAttribute("class", inside ? "b03-mass-in" : "b03-mass-out");
      if (inside) {
        d += " L " + sx(k) + " " + sy2(cum);
        cum += counts[i] / total; cumCount += counts[i];
        d += " L " + sx(k) + " " + sy2(cum);
        parts.push(counts[i] + "/" + total);
      }
    });
    d += " L " + sx(a) + " " + sy2(cum);
    step.setAttribute("d", d);
    line.setAttribute("x1", sx(a)); line.setAttribute("x2", sx(a));
    dot.setAttribute("cx", sx(a)); dot.setAttribute("cy", sy2(cum));
    aText.textContent = a.toFixed(1);
    valueText.textContent = "F(" + a.toFixed(1) + ") = " + cum.toFixed(3);
    if (parts.length === 0) {
      sumText.textContent = "No possible number of sharks lies at or below " + a.toFixed(1) + ", so F(" + a.toFixed(1) + ") = 0.";
    } else {
      const sumPart = parts.length > 1 ? parts.join(" + ") + " = " + cumCount + "/" + total + " ≈ " : parts[0] + " ≈ ";
      sumText.textContent = "P(K ≤ " + a.toFixed(1) + ") = " + sumPart + cum.toFixed(3) +
        ". About " + (100 * cum).toFixed(1) + "% of the deals have at most " + Math.floor(a + 1e-9) + (Math.floor(a + 1e-9) === 1 ? " shark." : " sharks.");
    }
  }
  slider.addEventListener("input", draw);
  draw();
})();
</script>

::: {#exm-b03-cdf-hand}
## Worked example: F(2) for the number of sharks, by hand

"$K\le 2$" contains the deals with one or two sharks, so add the first two
probability masses of the PMF. Of the 882 deals, 648 have one shark and 203
have two:

$$
F_K(2)=p_K(1)+p_K(2)
=\frac{648}{882}+\frac{203}{882}
=\frac{851}{882}\approx0.965.
$$

About 96.5% of the deals have at most two sharks. This is the running total
from question 2 of the opening section.
:::

The code below builds the full running total in R. Each CDF value is the
current PMF value plus all earlier PMF values:

```{r}
#| label: b03-sharks-distribution
k_values <- as.numeric(names(sharks_pmf))
p_values <- as.numeric(sharks_pmf)
sharks_distribution <- data.frame(
  sharks = k_values,
  count = as.numeric(table(deals$number_sharks_in_deal)),
  pmf = round(p_values, 3),
  cdf = round(cumsum(p_values), 3)
)
sharks_distribution
```

The table has one row per possible number of sharks. The column `count`
gives the number of deals, `pmf` divides it by 882, and `cdf` adds up the
`pmf` column from the top down to the current row. The `cdf` column grows
from 0.735 to 0.965, 0.990, 0.993, and finally 1. Read the row for three
sharks as an example: 99.0% of the deals have at most three sharks. The
last value is 1 because every deal has at most five sharks.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b03-sharks-cdf
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "See the R code for this figure"
#| fig-cap: "The CDF of the number of sharks in a deal: a step graph that never falls. It is 0 below one shark, jumps at each possible value by that value's probability mass, and stays at 1 from five sharks on."
library(ggplot2)
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
deals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1)
sharks_pmf <- prop.table(table(deals$number_sharks_in_deal))
cdf_df <- data.frame(
  threshold = as.numeric(names(sharks_pmf)),
  cdf = cumsum(as.numeric(sharks_pmf))
)
# For the line only: a flat part at 0 before one shark and at 1 after five
step_df <- rbind(
  data.frame(threshold = 0, cdf = 0),
  cdf_df,
  data.frame(threshold = 6, cdf = 1)
)

ggplot(cdf_df, aes(x = threshold, y = cdf)) +
  geom_step(data = step_df, linewidth = 1, colour = "#009E73") +
  geom_point(size = 2.6, colour = "#17324D") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.3f", cdf)), vjust = -0.9, hjust = 0.9,
            size = 3.6, colour = "#17324D") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.08), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  labs(x = "Threshold a (number of sharks)", y = expression(F[K](a))) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )
```

Read @fig-b03-sharks-cdf from left to right. Below one shark the line is
flat at 0, because no deal has fewer than one shark. At one shark it jumps
by 0.735, the share of deals with one shark. At two sharks it jumps by
0.230 to 0.965. The jumps at three, four, and five sharks are small: 0.025,
0.003, and 0.007. After five sharks the line stays at 1, because every deal
has at most five sharks.

A CDF adds up probability as the threshold moves from left to right. It
can stay flat or rise, but it cannot fall. It equals 0 below the smallest
possible value and reaches 1 once it includes all possible values.
In @fig-b03-sharks-cdf the line is flat at 0 to the left of one shark and
flat at 1 to the right of five sharks.

For a discrete variable, the CDF is a step graph. It stays flat between
possible values and jumps at each value that has positive probability. A
larger jump means that this value has more probability.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check: read F(3) from the step graph

$F_K(3)=P(K\le 3)$ is the height of the step graph at threshold 3. The
deals with one, two, or three sharks number $648+203+22=873$, so
$F_K(3)=873/882\approx0.990$. Only 1% of the deals have four or five
sharks.
:::

The CDF also answers questions about intervals, such as "between two and
three sharks". $F_X(b)$ contains all probability up to $b$, and $F_X(a)$
contains all probability up to $a$. If $a<b$ and you take the second away
from the first, only the probability between $a$ and $b$ is left. So the
probability of an interval is a difference of two CDF values:

$$P(a<X\le b)=F_X(b)-F_X(a).$$

Note the two signs. The lower end $a$ is excluded, because its mass is part
of $F_X(a)$ and is taken away. The upper end $b$ is included. For example,
the probability that a deal has two or three sharks is
$$P(1<K\le 3)=F_K(3)-F_K(1)=\frac{873-648}{882}=\frac{225}{882}\approx0.255.$$
So 25.5% of the deals have two or three sharks. We use $a=1$, not $a=2$,
because the deals with exactly two sharks must stay in the result.

The same idea answers other common questions. Each line below uses the
`cdf` column of `sharks_distribution`, or the counts behind it.

| Question | As a probability | From the CDF | Result |
|---|---|---|---:|
| exactly two sharks | $P(K=2)$ | $F_K(2)-F_K(1)=\frac{851-648}{882}$ | 0.230 |
| at least two sharks | $P(K\ge 2)=P(K>1)$ | $1-F_K(1)=\frac{882-648}{882}$ | 0.265 |
| more than three sharks | $P(K>3)$ | $1-F_K(3)=\frac{882-873}{882}$ | 0.010 |
| three, four, or five sharks | $P(2<K\le 5)$ | $F_K(5)-F_K(2)=\frac{882-851}{882}$ | 0.035 |

The first line shows that the mass at one value is the jump of the CDF at
that value: 0.230 is the PMF value for two sharks. The second and third
lines use the complement rule of Lecture 2, $P(A^c)=1-P(A)$: "at least
two" is everything except "at most one". So about one deal in four involves
two or more sharks, only 3.5% involve three or more, and only about one deal
in a hundred involves more than three.
For a founder this means that a large investor group is rare, but a second
shark is a real possibility.

The deal indicator of @fig-b03-deal-pmf has a CDF with only two jumps:
one at 0, of size $1-p$, and one at 1, of size $p$. Written out:

$$
F_X(a)=
\begin{cases}
0, & a<0,\\
1-p, & 0\le a<1,\\
1, & a\ge1,
\end{cases}
$$

where $p=P(X=1)$. So $p_X(1)=P(X=1)=p$, while $F_X(1)=P(X\le1)=1$. The
PMF measures the mass at exactly 1. The CDF includes all mass up to and
including 1.

The PMF and the CDF describe a whole distribution, value by value. For
planning, you often want a shorter summary: one number for the centre and
one for the spread. The next two sections give these two numbers.

### Expectation is the distribution's weighted centre

<p class="concept-video"><strong>MIT explanation (review):</strong>
<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_yJsO5955ZE">05.8 Expectation</a>.</p>

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} A distribution can contain many possible values and probabilities. The
**expected value**, or expectation, summarises its centre in one number.
Values with larger probabilities receive more weight:

$$E[X]=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}x\,p_X(x).$$

The notation $E[X]$ is read "the expected value of $X$". The expected value
is also called the mean of $X$ and written $\mu$ (the Greek letter mu) or
$\mu_X$. The calculation multiplies each possible value by its probability
and adds the products. You can also see the result as the balance point of
the probability distribution: if the masses were weights on a ruler, the
ruler would balance at this point.

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="label">Definition</span>

**Expected value.** The probability-weighted average of the possible values
of $X$, written $E[X]$, $\mu$, or $\mu_X$. If you repeat the experiment
many times, the average of the observed values comes close to $E[X]$.
:::

This long-run meaning does not make the expected value a guarantee for a
single observation. The weighted average in question 3 at the start of the
lecture was this calculation: the expected number of sharks in a deal is about 1.32. No
single deal has 1.32 sharks, but over many deals the average number of
sharks per deal comes close to 1.32.

Before we use the Shark Tank data again, try the calculation once on a very
small invented distribution.

::: {#exm-b03-tiny-expectation}
## Worked example: expectation of a tiny PMF

Let $Y$ have support $\{0,1,2\}$ with masses

$$p_Y(0)=0.2,\qquad p_Y(1)=0.5,\qquad p_Y(2)=0.3.$$

This is a valid PMF: all masses are non-negative and $0.2+0.5+0.3=1$. Write
every product:

$$
E[Y]
=0\times0.2 \;+\; 1\times0.5 \;+\; 2\times0.3
=0 + 0.5 + 0.6
=1.1.
$$

Each possible value contributes its value times its probability. The sum,
1.1, is the balance point. Note that 1.1 is not in the support: $Y$
never equals 1.1.
:::

Now apply the same steps to the Shark Tank distributions. For the deal
indicator,

$$E[X]=0\times(1-p)+1\times p=p.$$

The value 0 contributes nothing to the sum, so only the mass at 1 is left.
The expected value of a 0/1 variable is therefore the probability of a 1.
The same holds for data. If you add up the 0/1 values of `deal_on_show`
over all 1,441 records, every deal counts 1 and every other record counts
0, so the sum is the number of deals, 882. Dividing by 1,441 gives the
share of deals. This is why the mean of a 0/1 variable equals its
proportion of 1s, and why the code above computed the deal rate as
`mean(sharks$deal_on_show)`. Here $E[X]=882/1441\approx0.612$: on average,
0.612 deals per recorded pitch, or 61.2% of the pitches.

For the number of sharks, the sum has five products, one for each possible
number of sharks. This is the weighted average of question 3 in the opening
section. By hand, with the exact fractions:

$$
E[K]=1\times\frac{648}{882}+2\times\frac{203}{882}+3\times\frac{22}{882}
+4\times\frac{3}{882}+5\times\frac{6}{882}
=\frac{648+406+66+12+30}{882}=\frac{1162}{882}\approx1.32.
$$

The numerator has a simple meaning: the 882 deals together involve 1,162
sharks. Dividing by the number of deals gives the average number of sharks
per deal. The code below does the same in R. It stores the possible values
in `k` and their masses in `p_k`. Then `sum(k * p_k)` multiplies each value
by its mass and adds the products. For comparison, it also computes $E[X]$
and the plain average of the column `number_sharks_in_deal`:

```{r}
#| label: b03-expectation
k <- as.numeric(names(sharks_pmf))
p_k <- as.numeric(sharks_pmf)

c(
  E_X = 0 * (1 - p_hat) + 1 * p_hat,
  E_K_from_pmf = sum(k * p_k),
  observed_mean_sharks = mean(deals$number_sharks_in_deal)
)
```

The output confirms the hand calculation: $E[X]\approx0.612$ and
$E[K]\approx1.32$. The expected value from the PMF equals the plain average
of the 882 deals, because the PMF gives every deal the same weight, $1/882$.
The section on the sample mean at the end of this lecture comes back to
this point.

The expected number of sharks is about 1.32, and no deal has 1.32 sharks.
An expectation is a probability-weighted average, so it need not be a
possible value of the random variable. The value 1.32 lies close to 1, because most of the
probability sits at one shark. It lies about a third of a shark above 1,
because the deals with two or more sharks pull the balance point to the
right.

### Expectation after transforming a variable

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} In business, the quantity you care about is often not the random variable
itself but something computed from it. An investor does not care about the
number of units a start-up sells, but about the payoff that follows from
it. A shop owner cares about the profit, not the number of customers. A
founder with several sharks cares about the time spent keeping all of them
informed. In each case a fixed rule turns the random variable into the
quantity of interest.

Finance gives a second reason. An investor who compares a risky payoff
with a safe one wants to know how far the payoff can lie from its expected
value. A risky investment must offer a higher expected payoff than a safe
one, otherwise nobody would take the risk. This extra expected payoff is
called the risk premium. To measure the risk, we need the expectation of a
squared distance from the mean. That is again a value computed from the
random variable, and the section on variance builds on it.

Examples for the variable $Y$ of the worked example are the profit $10Y-3$
(10 euros per unit of $Y$ minus a fixed cost of 3 euros) and the square
$Y^2$. Such a function $g(X)$ of a random variable $X$ is itself a random
variable, with its own possible values and its own distribution.

If $g$ changes each possible value of $X$, the expected value of the
transformed variable is

$$E[g(X)]=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}g(x)\,p_X(x).$$

The probabilities do not change. Apply $g$ to each possible value, weight
the transformed values by the original PMF, and add.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Try it: E[Y²] for the tiny PMF

Use the same distribution as in the worked example: $Y\in\{0,1,2\}$ with masses $0.2,0.5,0.3$, and $g(y)=y^2$.

*Step 1 (given).* Square each possible value: $0^2=0$, $1^2=1$, $2^2=4$.

*Step 2 (you).* Multiply each squared value by its original probability
and write the three products.

*Step 3 (you).* Add them to get $E[Y^2]$. Is it equal to
$\left(E[Y]\right)^2=1.1^2$?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

$$
E[Y^2]=0\times0.2+1\times0.5+4\times0.3=0+0.5+1.2=1.7.
$$

It is not $\left(E[Y]\right)^2=1.21$. Squaring and then averaging
differs from averaging and then squaring. The gap between the two is
$1.7-1.21=0.49$. The section on variance gives this gap a name.
:::
:::

Now apply the same rule to the number of sharks. Take two functions of $K$.
The square $K^2$ is needed for the variance in the next section. The
number of pairs of sharks, $K(K-1)/2$, measures how much coordination a
deal needs. With one shark there is no pair, with two sharks there is one
pair who must agree, and with three sharks there are already three pairs.
The code below applies each function to the possible values in `k`,
weights the results by the original masses `p_k`, and adds them:

```{r}
#| label: b03-transformed-expectation
E_K <- sum(k * p_k)
c(
  E_K = E_K,
  E_K_squared = sum(k^2 * p_k),
  E_pairs = sum(k * (k - 1) / 2 * p_k),
  pairs_at_E_K = E_K * (E_K - 1) / 2
)
```

The first number repeats $E[K]\approx1.32$ from the previous section. By hand, $E[K^2]=(1\times648+4\times203+9\times22+16\times3+25\times6)/882
=1856/882\approx2.10$. This number has no direct meaning in sharks, but the
next section uses it. The expected number of pairs is about 0.39 per deal.
If you plug the expected number of sharks into the pair formula instead,
as in the last number of the output, you get $1.32\times0.32/2\approx0.21$,
only about half of the correct value.
The reason is the same as in the Try it task: the expectation of a function
is not the function of the expectation, except for straight-line rules. The
rare deals with four or five sharks have 6 or 10 pairs, and they count with
their full weight only in $E[g(K)]$. For straight-line rules such as profit
$10Y-3$, the next sections show that you may plug in the expected value.

### Variance and standard deviation

<p class="concept-video"><strong>MIT explanation (review):</strong>
<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZWo1XgAQE5k">06.2 Variance</a>.</p>

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Expectation gives the centre of a distribution, but it does not describe
how close the values lie to that centre. Two distributions can have
the same expectation and very different spreads. Both distributions in
@fig-b03-same-mean-spread have expectation 1. Which one is riskier, and
why?

```{r}
#| label: fig-b03-same-mean-spread
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "See the R code for this figure"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.15
#| fig-cap: "Two distributions with the same expectation and very different spreads. The dashed line marks the common mean, 1."
library(ggplot2)
spread_df <- data.frame(
  x = rep(0:2, times = 2),
  probability = c(0.10, 0.80, 0.10,    # Distribution A
                  0.45, 0.10, 0.45),   # Distribution B
  distribution = rep(c("Distribution A (variance = 0.20)",
                       "Distribution B (variance = 0.90)"), each = 3)
)

ggplot(spread_df, aes(x = x, y = probability)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "#C98B2E",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = x, yend = 0),
               linewidth = 1.1, colour = "#009E73") +
  geom_point(size = 2.6, colour = "#009E73") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.1, y = 0.87, label = "mean = 1",
           hjust = 0, colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ distribution) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:2) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.9),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "Possible value of X", y = "Probability") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D"),
    strip.text = element_text(colour = "#17324D", face = "bold")
  )
```

The horizontal axis lists the possible values and the vertical axis gives
their probabilities. The centre is the same, but Distribution B has greater
spread because values 0 and 2 receive much more probability. If these were
payoffs, B would be the riskier choice. Variance is the number that measures
this difference.

To measure spread, start with the deviation $X-\mu$, where $\mu=E[X]$.
If we averaged the deviations directly, positive and negative deviations
would cancel each other. So the **variance** squares each deviation before it
takes the probability-weighted average:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(X)
=E[(X-\mu)^2]
=\sum_x (x-\mu)^2\,p_X(x).
$$

The variance is also written $\sigma^2$, read "sigma squared" ($\sigma$ is
the Greek letter sigma). Read the calculation as four steps:

1. Find the centre, $\mu=E[X]$.
2. Measure each possible deviation, $x-\mu$.
3. Square the deviation, $(x-\mu)^2$.
4. Weight it by $p_X(x)$ and add across the support.

So large deviations contribute more than small deviations. Every term in
the sum is a square times a probability, so it can never be negative. The
variance is therefore always zero or positive.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Think about it: when is the variance zero?

The variance is a sum of terms $(x-\mu)^2\,p_X(x)$ that are all zero or
positive. When can the sum be exactly zero? Think of a business example of
such a variable before you open the answer.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

The sum is zero only if every term is zero. A term with positive
probability is zero only if $x=\mu$. So the variance is zero only when all
probability lies at one single value: the variable is not random at all.
An example is a fixed monthly rent of 800 euros. It equals 800 every month,
so its expected value is 800 and its variance is 0. Any chance of a
different value, however small, makes the variance positive.
:::
:::

There is a second way to compute the variance, called the **shortcut
formula** (also known as the computational form):

$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[X^2]-\left(E[X]\right)^2.$$

In words: the variance is the average of the squares minus the square of
the average. You compute two expectations from the PMF, $E[X^2]$ and $E[X]$,
square the second one, and subtract. This saves work, because you do not
need the deviation of every value from $\mu$. You met the gap between the
two numbers in the Try it task: $E[Y^2]=1.7$ and $\left(E[Y]\right)^2=1.21$
differ by 0.49. The shortcut formula says that this gap is exactly the
variance. It follows from the definition by multiplying out the square
$(X-\mu)^2=X^2-2\mu X+\mu^2$ and taking the expectation of each part. The
two formulas always give the same result. Use the shortcut formula to
calculate, and the definition $E[(X-\mu)^2]$ to interpret: the definition
shows that the variance is an average squared distance from the mean.

The **standard deviation** is the square root of the variance. It is also
written $\sigma$:

$$\operatorname{SD}(X)=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.$$

Variance has squared units. Standard deviation returns to the units of $X$.
If $X$ is measured in sharks, $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ is in sharks
squared, a unit that nobody can imagine, while $\operatorname{SD}(X)$ is
back in sharks.

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="label">Definition</span>

**Variance and standard deviation.** The variance, $\operatorname{Var}(X)$
or $\sigma^2$, is the probability-weighted average of the squared deviations
of $X$ from its mean $\mu$. The standard deviation, $\operatorname{SD}(X)$ or
$\sigma$, is the square root of the variance and has the same units as $X$.
:::

::: {#exm-b03-tiny-variance}
## Worked example: variance of the tiny PMF, both ways

Same $Y$ as before: values $0,1,2$ with masses $0.2,0.5,0.3$, and
$\mu=E[Y]=1.1$.

**By the definition**, in four steps:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=(0-1.1)^2(0.2)+(1-1.1)^2(0.5)+(2-1.1)^2(0.3)
$$
$$
=1.21\times0.2+0.01\times0.5+0.81\times0.3
=0.242+0.005+0.243
=0.49.
$$

**By the shortcut formula**, using $E[Y^2]=1.7$ from the Try it task:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)=E[Y^2]-\left(E[Y]\right)^2=1.7-1.21=0.49.
$$

Both ways give 0.49, so $\operatorname{SD}(Y)=\sqrt{0.49}=0.7$, in the
same units as $Y$.
:::

Now return to the number of sharks. The code below computes its variance
by the definition. It stores the expected value in `mu_k`, squares the
deviation of each possible value from it, weights the squares by `p_k`, and
adds them. It then checks the result with the shortcut formula and takes
the square root for the standard deviation:

```{r}
#| label: b03-variance
mu_k <- sum(k * p_k)
var_k <- sum((k - mu_k)^2 * p_k)

c(
  Var_K = var_k,
  Var_K_shortcut = sum(k^2 * p_k) - mu_k^2,
  SD_K = sqrt(var_k)
)
```

By hand with the shortcut formula and the numbers of the previous section:
$\operatorname{Var}(K)=E[K^2]-\left(E[K]\right)^2\approx2.104-1.317^2
=2.104-1.736\approx0.37$ sharks squared. Both ways give the same variance.
Its square root is the standard deviation, about 0.61 sharks. The number of
sharks in a deal typically lies about 0.6 sharks away from the expected
1.32, less than one shark and less than half of the expected value. This
answers the opening question: the number of sharks differs little from
deal to deal.

What does this mean for your own plans? If your pitch ends in a deal, you
might expect to work with one shark, and you should be prepared for a
second one: one deal in four has two or more sharks. A group of three or
more sharks is rare, with a probability of 3.5%. This forecast assumes
that your deal behaves like a deal drawn at random from the recorded deals.
If your company is unusually large or needs several kinds of expertise,
more sharks may want to join, and the recorded shares may not fit your
case.

Now return to the prediction question from before class. Option A pays €100
for sure, and Option B pays €0 or €200 with probability one half each. These
are the choices "keep it" and "go all-in" from the money question of the
Lecture 1 survey. The expected payoffs are equal:
$E[A]=100$ euros and $E[B]=0\times0.5+200\times0.5=100$ euros. Option A has
no spread at all, so $\operatorname{Var}(A)=0$. For Option B, both possible
payoffs lie 100 euros from the mean, so
$\operatorname{Var}(B)=(0-100)^2\times0.5+(200-100)^2\times0.5=10{,}000$
euros squared, and $\operatorname{SD}(B)=100$ euros. A typical result of B
lies 100 euros away from its expected payoff, which is as large as the
expected payoff itself. So the answer is: equal expected payoffs, and B is
the riskier option. The expectation alone cannot tell the two options apart.
Risk is the spread of the possible outcomes around the expectation, and the
variance and the standard deviation measure it. This is why investors and
founders look at both numbers when they compare an investment or a business
plan.

Expectation and variance are powerful summaries. For some distributions,
these two numbers even describe the whole distribution, so you do not need
the full PMF. Such distributions are so common in practice that they have a
name. The simplest example has only the values 0 and 1. You have already
seen one: the deal indicator $X$ of @fig-b03-deal-pmf. Many business
variables have this form: a customer buys or not, a loan is repaid or not,
a pitch reaches a deal or not.

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="label">Definition</span>

**Bernoulli distribution.** A random variable $X$ that takes only the values
0 and 1, with $P(X=1)=p$ and $P(X=0)=1-p$, has a Bernoulli distribution,
written $X\sim\text{Bernoulli}(p)$. Its expected value is $p$ and its
variance is $p(1-p)$.
:::

The symbol $\sim$ is read "is distributed as". A single number, $p$, fixes
the whole PMF. We found the expected value $p$ in the section on
expectation. The variance follows from the shortcut formula. Since $X^2=X$
when $X$ is 0 or 1 ($0^2=0$ and $1^2=1$), $E[X^2]=E[X]=p$, so

$$
\operatorname{Var}(X)=p-p^2=p(1-p).
$$

The deal indicator is a Bernoulli variable with $p=882/1441\approx0.612$.
The code below applies the two formulas to `p_hat`:

```{r}
#| label: b03-bernoulli-variance
c(
  E_X = p_hat,
  Var_X = p_hat * (1 - p_hat),
  SD_X = sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat))
)
```

The variance is $0.612\times0.388\approx0.237$ and the standard deviation
is about 0.49. A 0/1 variable lies either 0.612 below its mean (no deal) or
0.388 above it (deal), so a standard deviation of about one half is
natural. The variance $p(1-p)$ is largest when $p=0.5$, where it equals
0.25. With $p=0.612$ the deal indicator is close to this maximum: whether a
single pitch ends in a deal is nearly as uncertain as a coin toss.

### Shifting and rescaling a variable {#b03-shift-rescale}

The previous section measured the spread of one variable. Business
quantities are often built from other quantities: revenue is price times
units, profit is revenue minus a fixed cost. You do not need a new PMF to
find their centre and spread. For a straight-line rule $aX+b$ with
constants $a$ and $b$,

$$
E[aX+b]=aE[X]+b,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X),
$$
$$
\operatorname{SD}(aX+b)=|a|\operatorname{SD}(X).
$$

Adding a constant $b$ moves the centre and leaves the spread unchanged.
Multiplying by $a$ multiplies the centre by $a$ and the standard deviation
by $|a|$, the size of $a$ without its sign. So the variance is multiplied
by $a^2$.

The tiny PMF shows how each rule works. Let $Y$ be the number of units
sold on one day, with $E[Y]=1.1$, $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=0.49$, and
$\operatorname{SD}(Y)=0.7$. The table applies four rules to $Y$. The
probabilities 0.2, 0.5, and 0.3 stay the same in every row. Only the
possible values change.

| Rule | Business meaning | Possible values | Expected value | Variance | SD |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| $Y$ | units sold | 0, 1, 2 | 1.1 | 0.49 | 0.7 |
| $Y+2$ | two pre-ordered units are added every day | 2, 3, 4 | 3.1 | 0.49 | 0.7 |
| $2Y$ | every sale is a pack of two units | 0, 2, 4 | 2.2 | 1.96 | 1.4 |
| $-Y$ | units taken out of stock | $-2$, $-1$, 0 | $-1.1$ | 0.49 | 0.7 |
| $10Y-3$ | profit in euros: 10 euros per unit, 3 euros fixed cost | $-3$, 7, 17 | 8 | 49 | 7 |

Read the rows one by one. Adding 2 moves every value, and the centre, two
units to the right. The distances between the values do not change, so the
spread stays the same. Doubling doubles every value and every distance from
the mean. The standard deviation doubles from 0.7 to 1.4, and the variance,
which uses squared distances, grows four times, from 0.49 to 1.96. You can
check this with the definition: $E[2Y]=0\times0.2+2\times0.5+4\times0.3=2.2$,
and $\operatorname{Var}(2Y)=(0-2.2)^2(0.2)+(2-2.2)^2(0.5)+(4-2.2)^2(0.3)
=0.968+0.02+0.972=1.96$. Changing the sign mirrors the distribution: the
centre moves to $-1.1$, but the spread stays the same. This is why the rule
uses $|a|$ and $a^2$, which are never negative.

The last row combines both steps. If each unit of $Y$ earns 10 euros and
there is a fixed cost of 3 euros, the profit is $10Y-3$. Its expectation is
$10\times1.1-3=8$ euros. Its variance is $10^2\times0.49=49$ euros
squared, and its standard deviation is $10\times0.7=7$ euros, close to the
expected profit itself. So a typical day can lie far from the expected 8
euros. The fixed cost lowers the expected profit, but it does not make
profit more or less risky.

Standardising in [Lecture 6](b06-continuous-normal.qmd) uses this rule. Subtract the mean $\mu$ from $X$ and divide by the standard deviation
$\sigma$. The result $(X-\mu)/\sigma$ then has mean 0 and standard
deviation 1. Lecture 8 uses the same rules to find the spread of a sample
mean.

### Model expectation and the sample mean

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} The expected number of sharks turned out to equal the plain average of the
882 deals. This is no coincidence, and it raises a question that matters
for every analysis of data: when is a number a property of a probability
model, and when is it a summary of observed data? This section keeps the
two apart, because later lectures use the data to learn about the model.

For observed values $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, the sample mean is

$$\bar{x}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i.$$

Now give every observed row the same probability, $1/n$. This distribution
is called the **empirical distribution** of the data. Its expectation is

$$\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\,\frac{1}{n}=\bar{x}.$$

The two numbers are equal, but the two terms have different meanings. Expectation
describes a probability distribution. The sample mean summarises observed
data.

The same difference exists for spread. The variance of the empirical
distribution weights each of the $n$ observations by $1/n$, so it divides
by $n$. The usual **sample variance** divides by $n-1$:

$$s^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\left(x_i-\bar{x}\right)^2.$$

Its square root $s$ is the sample standard deviation. R's `var()` and `sd()`
divide by $n-1$. [Lecture 7](b07-samples-estimators.qmd) explains why we divide
by $n-1$ when we estimate a population variance.

An invented example shows the calculation by hand. A founder counts the
orders on five days: 3, 5, 6, 8, and 8. The mean is $\bar x=30/5=6$ orders.
The deviations from the mean are $-3$, $-1$, $0$, $2$, and $2$. Their
squares add up to $9+1+0+4+4=18$. Divide by $n-1=4$:
$s^2=18/4=4.5$ orders squared, so $s=\sqrt{4.5}\approx2.12$ orders. A
typical day lies about two orders, or about a third of the mean, away from
the mean. Dividing by $n=5$ would give $3.6$ instead of $4.5$. R gives the
same numbers:

```{r}
#| label: b03-small-sd
orders <- c(3, 5, 6, 8, 8)
c(mean = mean(orders), var = var(orders), sd = sd(orders),
  var_divide_n = mean((orders - mean(orders))^2))
```

The code below computes both versions for the number of words in the written description (`description_words`) in the
Shark Tank file:

```{r}
#| label: b03-word-mean-variance
w <- sharks$description_words
c(
  mean_words = mean(w),
  empirical_expectation = sum(w * rep(1 / length(w), length(w))),
  empirical_variance_divide_n = mean((w - mean(w))^2),
  sample_variance_divide_n_minus_1 = var(w),
  sample_sd = sd(w)
)
```

Both centre calculations give about 5.0 words for these 1,441 records. The
two variances, 3.647 and 3.649, differ only in the third decimal because $n$
is large. All these numbers summarise the same observations. To use one of
them as an estimate for a larger population, you also need to know how the
sample was drawn. Lecture 7 covers this. There, the model quantities $\mu$
and $\sigma^2$ of this lecture become the parameters of a population: fixed
numbers that describe the whole population. The data quantities $\bar x$ and
$s^2$ become statistics: numbers calculated from a sample. The first figure
of Lecture 7 shows how the model quantities and the data quantities are
connected.

::: {.caveat-box}
<span class="label">What an expected value can and cannot promise</span>

- An expected value is not a promise for one case. No deal has 1.32 sharks,
  and no pitch gets "0.612 of a deal".
- Single outcomes can lie far from the expected value. The standard deviation
  says how far, typically.
- All numbers here describe the recorded pitches. For future pitches they are
  only forecasts, and these forecasts depend on the assumptions of Lecture 2.

**What you can do with it:** plan with the expected value when a decision
repeats many times, and look at the spread when one bad outcome would cause
serious damage.
:::

### Answering the driving question

The driving question asked how many sharks you will work with if your pitch
ends in a deal, and how much that number differs from deal to deal.

How many sharks? Most likely one: 73.5% of the recorded deals have exactly
one shark. The expected number is 1.32 sharks per deal. No single deal has
1.32 sharks, but over many deals the average comes close to it.

How much does the number differ? Little. The standard deviation is about
0.61 sharks, less than half of the expected value, and 96.5% of the deals
have at most two sharks.

What does this mean for you as a pitcher? Plan for one shark as your
partner, but prepare for a second one: about one deal in four (26.5%) has
two or more sharks. A group of three or more is rare (3.5%). This
prediction assumes that your deal is like a deal drawn at random from the
recorded deals. If your company differs from the typical company on the
show, for example because it needs the expertise of several investors,
these shares may not fit your case. Lecture 4 shows how such information
changes the probabilities. In any case, the expected value alone would not
tell you all of this. Centre and spread together describe a distribution,
and one of them alone can give a wrong picture.

::: {.founder-box}
<span class="label">A founder's decision (invented example)</span>

Your lunch start-up sells boxes with prepared meals. Tomorrow you sell 20
meal boxes with probability 0.2, 30 with probability 0.5, and 40 with
probability 0.3. A meal box that you prepare but do not sell costs you 3
euros of ingredients. A customer that you cannot serve costs you 5 euros of
margin. How many meal boxes should you prepare: 20, 30, or 40?

Try it yourself first, in three steps.

1. Calculate the expected demand and its standard deviation.
2. For each plan, calculate the cost for each possible demand.
3. Weight these costs by the probabilities. This gives the expected cost of
   each plan.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## See the solution

**Step 1.** The expected demand is
$$E[X]=0.2\times20+0.5\times30+0.3\times40=31\text{ meal boxes}.$$
The variance is
$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(X)&=0.2\times(20-31)^2+0.5\times(30-31)^2\\
&\quad+0.3\times(40-31)^2\\
&=24.2+0.5+24.3=49,
\end{aligned}
$$
so the standard deviation is $\sqrt{49}=7$ meal boxes.

**Step 2.** If you prepare more than you sell, each box left over costs 3
euros. If you prepare fewer, each customer you turn away costs 5 euros. For
example, if you prepare 20 and the demand is 30, you turn away 10 customers,
which costs $10\times5=50$ euros.

| Plan | Demand 20 (probability 0.2) | Demand 30 (probability 0.5) | Demand 40 (probability 0.3) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Prepare 20 | 0 | $10\times5=50$ | $20\times5=100$ |
| Prepare 30 | $10\times3=30$ | 0 | $10\times5=50$ |
| Prepare 40 | $20\times3=60$ | $10\times3=30$ | 0 |

**Step 3.** The expected cost of a plan is the probability-weighted average
of its row, in euros per day:

- prepare 20: $0.2\times0+0.5\times50+0.3\times100=55$
- prepare 30: $0.2\times30+0.5\times0+0.3\times50=21$
- prepare 40: $0.2\times60+0.5\times30+0.3\times0=27$.

The decision: prepare 30 meal boxes, the plan with the lowest expected
cost. The expected demand of 31 told you where to aim. The spread of 7 meal
boxes and the two costs told you how much a wrong guess costs. Because a
lost customer costs more than a box left over, preparing 40 is cheaper than
preparing 20.
:::
:::

**Next:** We can now say what a typical pitch looks like and how much pitches
vary around it. But those are answers about a pitch we know nothing about.
In practice we always know something: its season, its industry, or the
rating of an AI tool that screens pitches. Lecture 4 asks how probabilities
change when new information arrives. It covers conditional probability and
the total-probability rule, which rebuilds an overall rate from group rates.
It also covers Bayes' rule, which reverses the direction of a question, and
independence, the case in which new information changes nothing.

:::

## After class

After the lecture, work through all the practice below.

### Read the lecture material

Read the Lecture material section above from start to end. The lecture
covered the most important parts. The text has every step, every example, and all the
code, including parts that were not shown in class. Note what is still
unclear and bring it to the next tutorial, or ask Tilly.

### Recall questions

1. What information does a PMF add to the support of a random variable?
2. Which two rules must every PMF follow?
3. What is the difference between $p_X(x)$ and $F_X(x)$?
4. Why can an expectation be a value the random variable never takes?
5. What does the variance average, and why do we square the deviations first?
6. Why do variance and standard deviation have different units, and which
   one is easier to interpret?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answers

1. The support lists possible values. The PMF gives a probability to each
   value.
2. Every probability mass is non-negative, and the masses sum to 1.
3. $p_X(x)=P(X=x)$ is the mass at exactly $x$. $F_X(x)=P(X\le x)$ is all
   probability accumulated up to and including $x$.
4. Expectation is a probability-weighted average and need not belong to the
   support.
5. Variance averages squared deviations from the distribution mean. The
   probability-weighted raw deviations sum to zero. Squaring prevents
   positive and negative deviations from cancelling each other.
6. Variance is in squared units of $X$. The standard deviation is its
   square root and returns to the units of $X$, which makes it the easier
   summary to interpret.
:::

### Finish a half-worked example

Re-read the two tiny-PMF worked examples (@exm-b03-tiny-expectation and
@exm-b03-tiny-variance). Then do all the steps on a new invented
distribution. Let $W$ have support $\{0,1,2\}$ with masses $0.3$, $0.4$,
and $0.3$.

*Step 1 (given).* Validity: all masses are non-negative and
$0.3+0.4+0.3=1$.

*Step 2 (you).* Calculate $F_W(1)$.

*Step 3 (you).* Calculate $E[W]$, writing each product.

*Step 4 (you).* Calculate $E[W^2]$, then $\operatorname{Var}(W)$ with the
shortcut formula, then $\operatorname{SD}(W)$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

$F_W(1)=P(W\le1)=0.3+0.4=0.7$.
$E[W]=0(0.3)+1(0.4)+2(0.3)=1.0$.
$E[W^2]=0(0.3)+1(0.4)+4(0.3)=1.6$, so
$\operatorname{Var}(W)=1.6-1.0^2=0.6$ and
$\operatorname{SD}(W)=\sqrt{0.6}\approx0.77$.
Compare $W$ with the variable $Y$ of the worked examples. Both take the
values 0, 1, and 2, but $W$ has the larger variance ($0.6>0.49$), because
more of its probability lies at the two ends, 0 and 2.
:::

### Practice

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Tasks 1 to 5 use the Shark Tank distributions of the lecture material.
Task 6 uses an invented example. In task 1, one of the 1,441
recorded pitches is selected at random. $X$ is the deal indicator: $X=1$ if
the pitch reached an on-air deal and $X=0$ otherwise. In tasks 2, 4, and 5,
one of the 882 deals is selected at random. $K$ is the number of sharks in
that deal (`number_sharks_in_deal`).

1. The deal indicator has $p=P(X=1)=882/1441$. Calculate $F_X(0.4)$.
2. Calculate $P(1<K\le4)$, the probability that a deal has two, three, or
   four sharks. Use the CDF table: the R output `sharks_distribution` in the
   section "A CDF accumulates probability up to a threshold".
3. A Bernoulli variable has $p=0.25$. Calculate its variance and standard
   deviation.
4. The standard deviation of the number of sharks $K$ is about 0.61. Write
   one sentence that interprets this number and names its units.
5. Why is $\operatorname{Var}(K)\approx0.37$ harder to interpret than
   $\operatorname{SD}(K)\approx0.61$?
6. An invented example. A founder sells phone cases at a weekend market.
   The number of cases sold on one day, $X$, has $E[X]=12$ and
   $\operatorname{SD}(X)=4$. Each case brings in 15 euros and the stall
   costs 60 euros per day, so the profit of one day is $15X-60$ euros.
   Calculate the expected value, the variance, and the standard deviation
   of the profit.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answers

1. Because $0\le0.4<1$, $F_X(0.4)=P(X=0)=559/1441\approx0.388$.
2. $P(1<K\le4)=F_K(4)-F_K(1)=(876-648)/882=228/882\approx0.259$. About 26%
   of the deals have two, three, or four sharks.
3. $\operatorname{Var}=0.25\times0.75=0.1875$.
   $\operatorname{SD}=\sqrt{0.1875}\approx0.43$.
4. The number of sharks in a randomly selected deal typically differs from
   the expected number (about 1.32) by roughly 0.6 sharks.
5. Variance is measured in sharks squared, a unit that is hard to imagine.
   The standard deviation is back in sharks.
6. Use the rules for $aX+b$ with $a=15$ and $b=-60$. The expected profit is
   $15\times12-60=120$ euros. $\operatorname{Var}(X)=4^2=16$, so the
   variance of the profit is $15^2\times16=3600$ euros squared. The standard
   deviation of the profit is $15\times4=60$ euros, half of the expected
   profit. The stall cost of 60 euros lowers the expected profit and leaves
   the spread unchanged.
:::

### Widget homework

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Open the [running-total lab](#cdf-lab) of
this lecture again. It uses the PMF of the number of sharks $K$ in a
randomly selected deal.

1. Set the threshold to $a=2.0$. Write down $F_K(2)$ and the masses that
   the lab adds up.
2. Move the slider slowly from 2.0 to 2.9. Does $F_K(a)$ change? Explain
   why.
3. Set $a=0.5$. What is $F_K(0.5)$, and why?
4. Use two readings of the lab to find $P(1<K\le3)$, the probability that
   a deal has two or three sharks.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check a model answer

1. $F_K(2)=648/882+203/882=851/882\approx0.965$. The masses at one and two
   sharks are added.
2. No. It stays at 0.965, because no possible number of sharks lies
   between 2 and 3. The CDF is flat between possible values and only jumps
   at them.
3. $F_K(0.5)=0$. No deal has fewer than one shark, so no probability lies
   at or below 0.5.
4. Read $F_K(3)\approx0.990$ and $F_K(1)\approx0.735$. The difference is
   $0.990-0.735=0.255$: about a quarter of the deals have two or three
   sharks.
:::

### Review questions from past lectures

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Select one of the 1,441 recorded pitches at random. $D$ is
the event of an on-air deal, and $L$ is the event of a late season (Seasons
9--16). Using the Lecture 2 counts table ($|D^c|=559$, $|L|=734$,
$|D^c\cap L|=229$, $n=1441$), calculate $P(D^c\cup L)$ and interpret it in
one sentence.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

$P(D^c\cup L)=(559+734-229)/1441=1064/1441\approx0.738$: about 74% of the
recorded pitches failed to reach an on-air deal, came from Seasons 9--16,
or both. We subtract the overlap (229 late-season no-deal records) once, so
that no record counts twice.
:::

### Worked exam interpretation

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} **Question.** Take the number of sharks in a deal
(`number_sharks_in_deal`) for the 882 Shark Tank pitches with an on-air deal.
For its distribution, R reports, after rounding, `expected_sharks` 1.32 and
`sd` 0.61. Interpret both numbers in
context, with their units.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check a model answer

The 1.32 is the expected number of sharks in a deal: the average of the
shark counts of the recorded deals, each count weighted by its share. No
deal has 1.32 sharks, because an expected value need not be a possible
value. The 0.61 is the standard deviation, in sharks. The number of sharks
in a deal typically differs from 1.32 by about 0.6 sharks, less than one
shark, so the number of sharks differs little between deals. Both numbers describe the
recorded deals. They do not guarantee the number of sharks for a future
pitch.
:::

### Worked exam interpretation: from a PMF to the standard deviation

**Exam-style question.** An invented example. A venture sells one product per customer,
at one of three prices. Let $V$ be the price paid by a randomly selected customer, in
euros, with PMF $p_V(10)=0.5$, $p_V(20)=0.3$, $p_V(40)=0.2$. (a) Verify
that this is a valid PMF. (b) Calculate $F_V(20)$. (c) Calculate $E[V]$
and $E[V^2]$. (d) Calculate $\operatorname{Var}(V)$ and
$\operatorname{SD}(V)$, stating the units of each.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check a model answer

&#40;a) All masses are non-negative and $0.5+0.3+0.2=1$.
&#40;b) $F_V(20)=P(V\le20)=0.5+0.3=0.8$.
&#40;c) $E[V]=10(0.5)+20(0.3)+40(0.2)=5+6+8=19$ euros.
$E[V^2]=100(0.5)+400(0.3)+1600(0.2)=50+120+320=490$.
&#40;d) $\operatorname{Var}(V)=490-19^2=490-361=129$ euros squared.
$\operatorname{SD}(V)=\sqrt{129}\approx11.4$ euros. The expected revenue
per customer is 19 euros. The typical deviation from it is about 11 euros,
more than half of the expected value.
:::

### Check the AI

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} You asked an AI assistant: "How many sharks will I work with if I get a deal?" It answered:

> "The expected number of sharks is 1.32. The expected value is the most likely value, so in most deals you negotiate with 1.32 sharks."

Find what is wrong and write the corrected answer. This is the **Verify**
step of Attempt → Ask → Verify → Explain.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

No deal has 1.32 sharks. The expected value is a weighted average, not the most likely value. The most likely number is one shark: 73.5% of deals have exactly one. The 1.32 is still useful, for example to plan for many deals, but it describes the centre of the distribution, not a single deal.
:::

### Make it yours

:::: {.utility-prompt}
<span class="label">Two sentences about your own venture</span>

Think of your own venture, or any business you know well. Pick one
uncertain quantity with a few possible values, for example the units
sold next week, the price a customer picks, or the orders per day. Sentence
1: describe its approximate PMF and give its expected value. Sentence 2: does
the centre or the spread matter more for a real decision you would make, and
why? There is no wrong answer.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## See an example, then write your own

Take a student-run venture that sells boxes of prepared meals on campus. "Daily orders next week are roughly 20 with probability 0.2, 30 with probability 0.5, and 40 with probability 0.3, so the expected value is about 31. The spread matters more than the centre for me, because I prepare ingredients in advance: a day with 40 orders when I have prepared for only 20 costs me more than an average day earns."
:::

You can discuss this task, and any other task in this chapter, with
Tilly for QM Basic, the course AI assistant: ask it to check whether your
PMF is valid and to compute its standard deviation with you.
